headline: New moon push at Race Point: mackerel stack thick, bass moving in underneath
subhead: The Bay's tightest tide cycle of the fall so far is squeezing bait against the bars from Provincetown to Billingsgate, and the stripers are starting to commit.
body_markdown:
The new moon that turned over September 10th put the strongest tidal push of the young fall season into Cape Cod Bay, and the fleet drifting Race Point and the outer bars this week has felt it in the current speed alone — water moving harder and longer through the rips than it has since spring. That kind of push does one thing reliably out here: it squeezes bait. Mackerel schools have been thick off the Point and along Peaked Hill Bars, rolling bait balls up tight against the bars on the ebb, and where the mackerel stack, the bigger predators aren't far behind. That's the read mates have been calling in from the radio all week, and it lines up with what we flagged last week — that bass would start committing hard to tightening bait schools as the moon built. That's exactly what's happening now, not scattered pickers anymore but fish making real decisions.

The better bass action has been concentrated on the last two hours of the ebb into dead slack at Race Point, where the rip stacks bait against the bar and stripers hold on the down-current edge waiting for the current to slack enough to feed comfortably. Boats working live mackerel — snagged right off the school with a bare treble and then fished on a fish-finder rig or freelined back into the rip — have taken bass up to the mid-30-pound class this week, with a scattering of fish pushing better than that on the days the mackerel schools held tightest to structure. Bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or olive over white, worked the same water on the drift when the mackerel weren't cooperating for live-lining, and they've produced enough fish in the 28 to 34-inch range to keep rods bent. The key has been patience through the hardest running water — most of the bite windows have been short, twenty to thirty minutes bracketing the slack, and boats that showed up mid-ebb and left before the tide eased missed it entirely.

Peaked Hill Bars has been holding a similar pattern in slightly shallower water, 15 to 25 feet over the bar itself, with bass working the sandy troughs between the humps on both the last of the ebb and the first hour of the flood. That spot has fished better for casters working topwater and darters at first light before the boat traffic pushes through, with bluefish mixed in — some solid 4 to 6-pound blues chopping through the same bait schools that are holding the stripers, a sign that the cooling nights are starting to concentrate adult blues rather than just the snapper-sized fish that have been thick in the harbors all summer.

Billingsgate has been more of a mixed bag. The fluke bite out there has been sliding the way it typically does this time of year — most of what's coming over the rail on the shoal itself is short, fish under 16 inches, while the better grade keeper fluke have already pushed off toward the deeper channel edges and the drop-offs on the Bay side of the flat. That's the classic late-season move: as the shallows hold onto summer warmth longer than the deeper water, the bigger fish slide off first looking for cooler structure, leaving juveniles to pick over the flats. Anyone still fluking Billingsgate is better served working the channel edges in 20 to 30 feet with Gulp on a light bucktail rather than grinding out shorts on the flat itself.

Cod remain mostly a story for later in the fall. A few boats working the deeper humps off Race Point on jigs have picked at a fish or two, but it's not a pattern yet — the water out there hasn't cooled enough to concentrate them the way it will once we get into October. Worth keeping in the back pocket, not worth planning a trip around just yet.

Sandy Neck and the Barnstable side have been quieter for stripers but steady for bluefish, with snapper blues thick in the harbors and creek mouths — a reliable sign, based on thirty years of watching this pattern repeat, that the adult run tightens up behind them as the water keeps cooling. Boats working peanut bunker on light tackle along the Neck have picked at some slot-sized bass on the outgoing tide, nothing to write home about yet but enough to suggest the same bunker-and-mackerel dynamic playing out at Race Point is starting to show along the south shore of the Bay too.

Looking ahead, the moon is moving off new but the tidal push should stay elevated for another few days, which means the bait-tightening pattern at Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars likely holds through the weekend before starting to ease. If the wind stays out of the northwest in the mornings and lays down by midday — which has been the pattern lately — the slack-tide windows at the rip should keep producing on live mackerel and bucktails. If it swings onto the water from the southeast, expect the bite to get more compressed and harder to time. Either way, the mackerel are the tell right now — where they're stacked thick against the bars, that's where the time belongs.
